articles.title: Pakistan’s Russian dilemma
articles.content: IT is difficult to imagine a single small gesture reducing decades-old hostility between two archrivals. Yet, such a moment was witnessed recently when Alok Dimri, India’s national coordinator for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, visited Islamabad for a meeting. Talking to the state media, he said he was happy to be in Pakistan. It was a simple statement, but perhaps one that may ease some of the cross-border bitterness. Mr Dimri said this while visiting the National Council of Arts in Islamabad. The heritage, art, and culture that Pakistan and India share have repeatedly fallen victim to toxic narratives designed to provoke hate. Yet the cultural link carries a powerful sense of mutual belonging. It may be premature to read too much into the Indian delegate’s visit or to view his words as evidence of a thaw after lastMay’s stand-off. Still, the episode offers some hope: if leaders on both sides choose to move forward, the dialogue could quickly regain momentum. However, optimism should be tempered — as should any expectation that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi will arrive in Islamabad to attend the SCO summit. If he did, it would be a miracle, and the biggest surprise in decades — even bigger than Rajiv Gandhi’s visit to Islamabad in 1988 to attend the Saarc summit or Atal Bihari Vajpayee’s arrival in Lahore in 1999. Both occasions had generated enormous hope for peace between the two neighbours. What actually followed is a familiar story. Another miracle would be if Russian President Vladimir Putin attended the Islamabad SCO summit next year. Pakistan is more curious about this visit and hopes it may trigger a major shift in its geopolitics and ambitions in Central Asia, while influencing the regional discourse in ways that would irritate India. Pakistan would be keen to enhance its defence cooperation with Russia, but particularly interested in making some progress on the much-discussed railway from Moscow to Islamabad and establishing a freight corridor using existing 7,000-kilometre-long railway networks, with Pakistan linked to Russia through Central Asia and/or Iran. Over the decades, Pakistan, the Central Asian states, and Iran have conceived many transnational projects, and each time with great enthusiasm, yet none has materialised. Afghanistan is always made to bear the burden of the blame because of its complex relationship with Pakistan. Russia is likely to remain cautious about deepening its cooperation with Pakistan. Is it not interesting that the conventional wars fought by India and Pakistan collectively may not have lasted for more than a few weeks, and that Pakistan fought its longest war against the Soviet Union in Afghanistan? Pakistan and the Afghan mujahideen, together with the US, defeated the Russians, which was followed by the dismantling of the Soviet state. The Pakistani leadership still takes pride in that success. Of course, times have changed, and Pakistan is looking to cultivate new economic and defence opportunities. Russia, however, is likely to remain cautious about deepening its cooperation with Pakistan. This is not because of their bitter past, from which both sides have moved on, but because of divergent regional interests, particularly over Afghanistan, and Russia’s deep and long-standing engagement with India. Russian-Indian defence and economic cooperation is not necessarily an obstacle to developing ties with Pakistan. But it does mean that Islamabad cannot be regarded as a preferred partner in that context. The disparity in economic relations is significant: Pakistan’s bilateral trade with Russia is less than half a billion dollars, compared with around $69bn in India-Russia trade. The gap is even more pronounced in defence cooperation. India maintains ahigh level of military engagementwith Russia through multiple military-technical cooperation frameworks, including joint research and development, co-development, co-production, and after-sales support. By contrast, Russia’s defence engagement with Pakistan remains selective and falls well short of a strategic military partnership. At the same time, India’s diversification of its defence partnerships has not significantly weakened its relationship with Russia. Moscow may have reservations about some aspects of New Delhi’s growing defence ties with other countries, but there are no clear signs of a fundamental deterioration in bilateral relations. Russia’s interest in Pakistan is, therefore, largely geopolitical — maintaining engagement with Islamabad allows Moscow to show that its international network of partnerships is broad, while also keeping channels open with Pakistan’s political and security leaders, including those who have close ties with US President Donald Trump. Public diplomacy is a domain through which Russia keeps its support club intact and seeks to enhance it, engaging Pakistani media, academics, opinion-makers, and policymakers through exchange programmes. The SCO is another platform Russia uses more extensively than other partners for public diplomacy. Russia and Pakistan share counterterrorism concerns, but their approaches to Afghanistan differ sharply. Russia has recognised the Taliban regime, but Pakistan is fighting a tough war against terrorism and sees Afghanistan as a source of the war. In geo-economic terms, they have different priorities. Russia wants Afghanistan in the camp of its Central Asian allies. At the same time, Pakistan is a major partner of the US in areas where the interests of the two countries converge in Afghanistan. This irritates not only Russia but also China, which wants the US to stay out of the region in its immediate neighbourhood. The US took two decades to leave Afghanistan, and China does not want to see it coming back. It is not surprising that Indian-Russian relations have had few hiccups over decades. At the same time, Pakistan chose the US as its strategic partner after independence. Still, their relationship has not been smooth. Pakistan’s strategic partnership with China has also been tested recently, triggered by CPEC-related disputes and internalsecurity concernsregarding Chinese nationals in Pakistan. Perhaps Russia is a new love interest for a segment of Pakistan’s power elite, but the two have little to share. And the last optimistic note: what if India and Pakistan decide to live in peace? What would the geopolitical impact be?
articles.author: Muhammad Amir Rana

articles.title: The court that could not see
articles.content: WITNESSES testified that a senior banker sketched private parts on the glass of his desk, asked a woman colleague to name them, and threatened to tear off her clothes if she wore a particular outfit again. Another officer made indecent remarks about her attire before colleagues. The ombudsperson found the charges proved; the Islamabad High Court agreed. On Sept 16, the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC)set that judgement asidewithout substantively engaging with this evidence or the high court’s careful appraisal of it. Its central reason was a definition. Harassment under the 2010 workplace harassment law, it declared, “is only restricted to conduct which is sexual in nature”. Even by that narrow test, the conduct proved was plainly sexual. Before the high court, the officers never contended it fell short of harassment. Why does the FCC confine harassment to sex? The Act’s title and preamble speak of ‘harassment’, not ‘sexual harassment’, and anchor it in the right to dignity. Nor does ‘sexual’ mean only the act of sex; it also means relating to the sexes, or to gender. The Supreme Court said so on review in Nadia Naz, through Justice Ayesha Malik; “sexually demeaning attitudes” means demeaning a person because of their sex. Yale’s Vicki Schultz has shown that much workplace harassment has nothing to do with desire; it belittles women and signals they do not belong. And the2022 amendment, ignored altogether, covers gender discrimination “which may or may not be sexual in nature”. Courts elsewhere agree. The US supreme court held in Oncale that harassment need not be motivated by desire; Canada and India root it in equality and dignity. India’s law lists “sexually coloured remarks”, exactly what was proved, and the 2021 Nadia Naz judgement the FCC relies on quoted that very provision. ILO Convention 190 treats gender-based harassment, including sexual harassment, as one wrong. This is where a constitutional court should begin. Article 14 declares the dignity of man inviolable, and the Act’s own preamble rests on it. A constitutional court’s first duty is to read statutes through fundamental rights and expand their frontiers, not shrink them. A woman made to name drawings of private parts before her colleagues has had her dignity violated by any measure. Constitutional courts are judged not by the powers they claim but by the rights they protect. Our Supreme Court had already arrived there. In Uzma Naveed (2022) and Muhammad Din (2025), both of which I authored, it held that harassment is not confined to the act of sex and that dignity is absolute and non-negotiable. The FCC dismisses Muhammad Din in one sentence, “with due respect”, ignores Uzma Naveed, and leans instead on the 2021 Nadia Naz judgement the Supreme Court set aside on review. In Haji Adam, decided by the same author the same day, substantial passages reappear word for word; it even names the bank case’s witnesses as the Pemra complainant’s. That raises a serious question whether each record received independent judicial consideration. Precedent is not a courtesy; it is law. Judgements of the Supreme Court delivered before the 27th Amendment bound every court under Article 189. The amendment operates prospectively: it makes the FCC’s decisions binding from now on, but it does not erase nearly eight decades of constitutional jurisprudence. Having inherited the Supreme Court’s constitutional jurisdiction, the FCC inherited the law declared under it. If it doubts that law, the doctrine of precedent requires reasoned reconsideration by a larger bench, not a three-member bench’s single sentence. Even the FCC’s own test, set this March, forbids precedent being “ignored and disregarded in silence”. The deeper problem is the court itself. It was created by the 27th Amendment, rushed through a parliament whose own mandate remains clouded by the disputed elections of February 2024, and carved out of a functioning Supreme Court for reasons never convincingly explained. Britain, the US, India, Canada and Australia entrust constitutional questions to a single apex court, and for good reason: splitting the apex invites conflict and political engineering. South Africa moved the other way in 2013, making its constitutional court the apex court in all matters. Its first bench was chosen by the president on the prime minister’s advice, bypassing the Judicial Commission, with no published criteria or open assessment of merit. Such a court must earn confidence through its work. A judgement rendered without hearing the attorney general or appointing an amicus (even the high court had one), and thin on scholarship and constitutional understanding, does not earn it. Nor does the price: salaries above the Supreme Court’s until that court was raised to match, generous staff allowances, and three more years of tenure. Not a single woman sits on the FCC, a conspicuous absence in a harassment case. I cast no aspersion on any judge who accepted appointment; that is for each conscience. Yet the absence speaks. The women of our judiciary stand apart from this court and deserve the country’s admiration. Such judgements belong to the bar too, for it is very much part of this new judicial era. Bar associations are guarantor institutions; in 2007 theymarcheduntil judges were restored. When the architecture of the 26th and 27th Amendments was assembled, that resistance never came. Too many at the bar’s helm measure ambition by proximity to power rather than fidelity to democracy. That is a deficit of character, not of numbers. When the guardians fall silent, unconstitutionalism rises. Constitutional courts are judged not by the powers they claim but by the rights they protect. If this is the direction of travel, dark years lie ahead for rights. Faiz urged us to speak while our lips are still free. It now falls to the lawyers who remember 2007, the academy and those who refuse to be silenced to keep the lamps lit. The writer is a former senior puisne judge of the Supreme Court of Pakistan, Professor of Practice at SAHSOL, Lums and currently a Visiting Fellow at Yale University, US.
articles.author: Justice (retd) Syed Mansoor Ali Shah

articles.title: Mao’s legacy
articles.content: LAST month, China marked Mao Zedong’s 50th death anniversary. He died on Sept 9, 1976. There is no limit to biographies on him, but one of the most authentic in English — Mao, the People’s Emperor — is by Dick Wilson. As the book rightly claims, Mao was “the most brilliant, the most controversial figure of this [20th] century, and the most enigmatic”. The ‘ease’ in writing about Mao is the abundance of information about him at every stage of his life. He wanted to go to school, but his martinet father wanted help with farm work. One day, he turned up at a school, but the security guard didn’t let him in because of Mao’s age and grown-up physique. Mao nevertheless made his way in, even though most students were bewildered by his presence amongst them. One key factor in Mao’s personal life was tragedy, which included the murder of his family members. Among them was his 29-year-old second wife,Yang Kaihui, the mother of their sons Anying, Anqing and Anlong. She was a member of the Chinese Communist Party and faced a firing squad. A brother, Mao Zemin, was tortured and executed. His youngest brother, Mao Zetan, was a talented man. He didn’t go on the Long March, and, instead, chose to organise guerrilla warfare against the government headed by Chiang Kai-shek. He fell while fighting. Also captured and killed was Mao Zejian, Mao’s adopted sister. Similarly, Mao Chuxiong, the son of Mao Zetan, was murdered and buried secretly. A lot of Mao’s peculiarities deserve to be noted. Other than what scholars write about one of the modern era’s great men, a lot of peculiarities about Mao deserve to be noted. For instance, during the historic Long March, he ordered that a word should be displayed or scrawled on the back of everyone, so that the person following him should learn it. It was his way of emphasising the importance of literacy. The Long March was truly a long march across 10,000 kilometres of plains, mountains and rivers. Those taking part consisted of three armies avoiding a clash with Chiang’s forces. It took them one year (1934-35) to reach Yanan in north-western China. The march began with around nearly 86,000 people, but less than 10,000 reached Yanan; the rest dying from hunger, illness, and exhaustion. Among the prominent people in the Long March were Zhou Enlai, who later became China’s foreign minister and premier, and Zhu De, who was among the founders of the Red Army and helped overthrow China’s last imperial government. Some 13 years after reaching Yanan, Mao Zedong felt strong enough to take Beijing, where he officially announced the formation of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) on Oct 1, 1949. He had entered Beijing on Jan 31, 1949 triumphantly and peacefully, because the Kuomintang’s (KMT) commanding officer, Gen Fu Zuoyi, had agreed to lay down arms. Thus, China’s capital city fell peacefully to Mao after a war that had killed an estimated 4.9 million people. As the virtual emperor of the world’s greatest country population-wise, Mao was keen to meet another ‘emperor’, who was the head of state of the globe’s biggest country territorially — Joseph Stalin. Details of their first meeting in Moscow on Dec 16, 1949, show a lack of warmth and hospitality on Stalin’s part. The Chinese guests were made to stay at places that were beneath the dignity of a delegation led by a head of state. Also, Stalin never invited them over to lunch or dinner and confined his hospitality to snacks. Many scholars, however, present an altogether different view and say Stalin couldn’t be so crude and undiplomatic. But the issue was more than diplomatic etiquette. What was bothering Stalin were larger geopolitical issues, for he didn’t feel happy about having a powerful neighbour in Russia’s east, while he faced America and Nato in the west. Mao was intelligent enough to realise that a delay in conquering the southern part of the country could create complications and encourage non-communist forces to join Chiang’s army. He lost no time, rejected a peace offer, and ordered the Red Army to cross the Yangtze River and capture Nanjing, the KMT capital. Shanghai, the economic hub, fell next. Guangzhou (Canton) followed. A spectacular achievement was the capture of Hainan, an island, by an amphibious invasion wiping out KMT rule from the Chinese mainland. Chiang Kai-shek then fled to Taiwan. Pakistan is lucky to have China as a neighbour and friend. During my visits to China, I found how the Chinese people remember that it was Pakistan that had brought the US and China together and that president Richard Nixon and Chairman Mao had their historic meeting on Feb 21, 1972, at Mao’s home in Beijing owing to Pakistan’s efforts. The writer is Dawn’s External Ombudsman and an author.
articles.author: Muhammad Ali Siddiqi

articles.title: Beyond Oct 7
articles.content: THREE years ago, Israel had most of the world’s sympathy. On Oct 7, 2023, Hamas-led fighters killed around 1,200 people in Israel and took more than 250 hostages. Israel experienced a kind of grief that Palestinians live with every day. But grief is not a blank cheque. Three years on, the story Israel told the world about itself that day no longer commands automatic authority. Oct 7 happened. But the world has spent three years watching what came after. Gaza’s health ministry now counts at least 74,000 Palestinians killed. More than 1,100 have died since a ceasefire took effect last October. Israeli forces still control over half the territory. In 2024, I wrote here about the Western media’s role in protecting Israel’s narrative — the different standards applied to Israeli and Palestinian victims, the lavish attention paid to Israeli suffering, the reduction of Palestinian deaths to statistics. Much of that criticism was dismissed as partisan. But what happens when audiences stop waiting for the media to tell them what they are seeing? Palestinians in Gaza have spent three years documenting their own destruction on their phones. Palestinian journalists have kept reporting through the same bombardment, hunger and displacement they cover. They have paid for it with their lives. The Committee to Protect Journalists says Israeli forces have killed 191 Palestinian journalists and media workers in Gaza. Foreign reporters, meanwhile, have been kept out. The result is an inversion of the old media hierarchy. For decades, Palestinians were spoken about rather than listened to. Their suffering was filtered through Israeli statements, Western correspondents and government briefings. Today, despite censorship and an enormous imbalance of power, they speak directly to the world. And the world is listening. What is Israel afraid the world will see? This matters because Israel’s most powerful argument after Oct 7 was not simply that it had been attacked. It was that everything it did next had to be viewed through the lens of victimhood. Hamas was condemned for murdering civilians and taking hostages. ‘Do you condemn Hamas?’ became the entry ticket to any Western conversation about Palestinian suffering. Condemnation was the toll everyone had to pay before they were allowed to mention Gaza. How often were Israeli officials asked to condemn anything before they spoke? Three years on, that formula has collapsed. You can condemn the killing of Israeli civilians and ask why Palestinian children have been killed in such numbers. You can oppose Hamas and oppose the occupation. These positions were never contradictory. Israel needed them to seem so. Its reputation is no longer being challenged only by activists, Arabs or Muslims. A 2026 Pew Research Centre survey across 36 countries found a median 67 per cent of respondents viewed Israel unfavourably, against 25pc who viewed it favourably. In the US, Israel’s most important ally, 60pc now hold an unfavourable view, up from 53pc a year ago. This is not the work of a marginal activist class. In 2024, I also wrote that younger audiences were abandoning legacy media for social media, podcasts and YouTube because they no longer trusted it to tell the story of Gaza honestly. That alternative ecosystem has only grown. The irony is that Israel’s attempts to control the story have destroyed its credibility. When foreign journalists cannot enter Gaza, when the journalists already there keep dying, and when Palestinians become the only witnesses to their own destruction, the absence of independent access becomes the story. What is Israel afraid the world will see? Israel can insist the world is being fed misinformation. It can call its critics antisemitic. It can say Hamas is responsible for civilian deaths because it hides among civilians. But repetition is not proof. That is the difference between Oct 7, 2023, and Oct 7, 2026. Three years ago, Israel’s trauma was the story. Today, the question is what Israel did with the world’s sympathy. The answer is being judged not by Israeli officials or their allies, but by audiences who have watched Gaza destroyed in real time. Israel still has enormous military power, diplomatic protection and powerful friends. But it has lost something no press conference or invocation of Oct 7 can restore: the assumption that its version of events will be believed. For Palestinians, this is not victory. Their homes are not rebuilt because opinion has shifted. Their dead do not return because the media is finally paying attention. Recognition does not end an occupation. Families still shelter in tents among the ruins. Israeli strikes continue, ceasefire or not. Sympathy has never stopped a bomb. But the story is no longer Israel’s alone to tell. Three years after Oct 7, that is the real story. The writer is a journalist and conducts writing workshops in Karachi.
articles.author: Muna Khan

articles.title: Yemen offensive
articles.content: IT appears that escalation is on the cards where the Houthi-Saudi and US-Iran conflicts are concerned. As per reports, Riyadh is planning an offensive to help the Yemeni government — which it backs — retake the strategically important Red Sea coast area from the pro-Iran Houthis, who captured it during a lightning offensive last month. Hostilities are continuing; there were reports on Saturday of bothRiyadh and Sana’a being attacked. Meanwhile, members of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement aredue to hold an emergency meetingto discuss the Yemen situation. Regarding Iran, the US has reportedly ordered thousands more troops, as well as an aircraft carrier group, to the Gulf. This mirrors the build-up of American forces around Iran before the US-Israeli assault targeted the Islamic Republic in late February. Top US officials have reportedly met at Camp David to discuss the Yemen and Iran files. Diplomacy, it seems, is giving way to more war in the Gulf and the wider Middle East. The humanitarian situation in Yemen is dire, with hundreds of thousands of people uprooted, while the UN says millions of Yemenis, including more than 2m infants, face acute hunger. If the Yemen war sucks in more regional states, it will complicate matters further. The best option, therefore, is for Muslim and Arab states to help restore the Saudi-Houthi ceasefire. The Houthi Ansarallah group must pledge to stop its attacks on Saudi Arabia, while ensuring free passage through Bab al-Mandeb. The Saudis, on their part, should consider lifting the blockade of Houthi territory, while encouraging all Yemeni factions to peacefully resolve the internal conflict. The Yemen war has been raging for over a decade, and previous external interventions have failed to end it; in fact, continued violence has exacerbated the humanitarian situation. With regard to Iran, it appears that President Donald Trump’s administration has halted kinetic action only till the November US midterms, and plans to restart hostilities after elections are out of the way. This would be a grave error. US-Israeli aggression has caused great loss of life in Iran as well as damage to infrastructure, while the global economy has been shell-shocked due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The world — particularly the states of the region — cannot afford more disruption and war. Mr Trump hasturned downthe recent Iranian proposal to open Hormuz. He should reconsider his strategy and restart dialogue with Tehran, while the Iranians should promise to reopen the strait if the US lifts its blockade of Iran and eases sanctions. The US leader has hailed the exit of American troops from Iraq. He should work on a similar plan to bring his forces home from elsewhere in the Gulf and end the Iran war.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Growth transition
articles.content: PRIME Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s recent call to move from stabilisation to growth, job creation and export promotion was overdue. But the danger lies in treating the shift as a change of direction rather than a change in the quality of economic policy. Mr Sharif said macroeconomic stability has been restored and the next task is growth driven by technology, production, employment and exports. He is not wrong. He pointed to rising reserves, remittances and IT exports, a return to the international debt market, and better investor confidence. He also admitted that industries protected by tariffs and subsidies have failed to become competitive. That contradiction lies at the heart of the growth challenge. Successive set-ups have pursued growth by distributing incentives rather than improving productivity. Tax breaks, subsidised credit, tariff protection, and preferential treatment have produced protected businesses, not globally competitive ones. That calls for distinguishing between growth and productive growth. A temporary expansion in construction, real estate or consumption can raise GDP. It cannot create foreign exchange earnings needed to sustain that expansion. Our recurring problem is that growth eventually runs into the external account. Imports rise, reserves come under pressure, and the country returns to stabilisation. That cycle must be broken. The IMF’s own assessment makes clear that macroeconomic stability remains a prerequisite, not an obstacle to growth. It has called for deeper reforms to improve governance, competition, productivity, the business environment, energy sector viability and human capital. It has also warned that unfinished structural reforms would leave Pakistan dependent on the public sector and vulnerable to renewed imbalances. This is why the language of a ‘shift’ needs careful handling. Stabilisation cannot simply be relaxed to create room for faster growth. The government still has to protect fiscal discipline, rebuild external buffers and keep inflation under control. The real transition to growth, therefore, should be from stabilisation through transformation. Growth cannot be proclaimed merely because the immediate crisis has eased. Growth must come from expanding globally competitive manufacturing, modernisation of agriculture, IT and services, and export-oriented SMEs. The test is whether the government can make growth durable rather than another short-lived expansion.
articles.author: Editorial
